headline: ‘I miss old Google’: readers tell us how they search the internet in the age of AI
trail_text: A feature called AI Overviews has been a profound change, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting
body_text: Google has put artificial intelligence at the front and center of its search bar. The most-visited site on the internet still shows the same list of links to users, but they have to scroll past a summarized response from an AI chatbot, a feature Google calls AI Overviews. The change to what was once the gateway to the rest of the internet has been profound, and the browsing habits of billions of people are shifting. “AI is driving the most significant upgrade of the Google Search experience ever,” wrote Liz Reid, Google’s vice-president of search, last August. In May, the company said more AI is coming. As people grow accustomed to AI chatbots, they’re spending more time with Google’s and therefore more time on Google.com. Academic studies are finding that people navigate less to sites beyond Google if an AI Overview can give them a good enough answer, even if the bot cites the sites that feed it. Clicks, also known as traffic, are often the most significant way a website earns money from advertising. Media outlets and website owners are enduring a sustained traffic decline. Large US media companies are suing Google, alleging that AI summaries have redirected and reduced traffic to their sites, cutting into their revenue. Google said it had not seen a decline in aggregate traffic and that such accusations are based on “flawed methodologies”. Reid, the company’s vice-president of search, wrote last year: “Total organic click volume from Google Search to websites has been relatively stable year-over-year.” The Guardian asked readers whether Google has improved or worsened in the age of AI and how their habits of searching the internet have changed. ‘Google is better now’ Better, mainly because it leads you in your quest rather than you having to search on yourself. I am happy to have the AI lead me to an answer but the mega caution is that Google AI or any of them are not at all trustworthy. I have had it admit that it was lying to me and apologise! Sionn Achog, retired teacher 76, Dublin I find that AI responses are more informative than previously, which simply referred the user to other relevant websites. Peter Warb, 75, UK AI has made Google better. I use AI mode for all my searches. Jose Garcia Jr, 40, recovery coach, Dallas, Texas AI has improved Google search. The analysis and chat functions are so much more useful than a ranked list of websites that still need to be explored by the user. Reviewing a list of websites is still an option but is very time consuming, and frustrating. Alan Caruana, consultant, 62, Malta Far more better, faster and real. I search now with confidence, complete assurance and a high degree of accuracy. Eleazar Eke, electrical engineer, 67, Onitsha, Nigeria Much better. It hasn’t changed my behavior, just getting better and more focused results. Catherine Weber, former political analyst, 57, Oregon It’s made Google search much better, I find that I rarely actually click on the website links any more. I find information I want much faster and have a deeper understanding of any topic as I can ask questions about it and drill into the areas I’m interested in. Mark Johnson, 52, software engineer, London Greatly improved it by getting at more arcane info regarding subject matter. Juxtaposition has improved with AI and abstruse knowledge of subjects becomes more accessible to layman. Wonderful tool with power to extend mind through sensing connections and very akin to human thinking. Samuel Lieberstein, 90, retired teacher, Cherry Hill, New Jersey ‘Search has gotten worse’ Search has become worse. Google AI obscures sources and tries to claim information it did not create while diverting traffic from the sources it steals from. Sean Peters, document processor, 41, Portland, Oregon Every time I search I have to scroll down to find an actual real website to find a full article or discussion or to confirm that the AI summary isn’t making things up. Occasionally when I am feeling particularly bitter, I remember to add the ““-ai”” tag to my search. Ewan Herbert, English teacher, 33, Japan Worse. I have disabled AI overviews using an extension. Chris Gibson, Dundee Absolutely worse. I want to be able to decide for myself which results are the most useful and relevant, and we’re no longer able to turn off the AI summary results. Jon Wilkinson, personal trainer, 43, Manchester, UK ‘It’s so bad I quit Google’ Google has been enshittified … I do miss old Google Search and I really hope something of equal capabilities eventually comes to replace it. The search engine I currently use is good for a lot of things, but if I need to look for something in languages other than English, the quality of the results is much lower. Image search is also not as good as that of Google used to be. Sofia, postdoctoral physics researcher, 30, Lausanne, Switzerland My first stop now is Duck Duck Go, a pale imitation of Google’s search engine at the height of its powers. Unfortunately, the top results often include Grokipedia entries and other garbage. Craig Garrett, book editor, 52, New York City I have stopped using Google. I now use another search engine with no AI overviews. Guy Arthur Simpson, writer 66, Spain I’ve made a conscious effort to find a browser which does not lead with the AI results. Mine is now Ecosia. Dan Jennings, IT, 54, Southampton, UK I do a lot of research for my studies, and the AI features are a nightmare! I’m still scouring for a decent search engine without any of these ‘AI features’, the last thing i want is to accidentally utilise a water-wasting AI behemoth datacentre when I forget that crucial suffix. I’ve even resorted to using my local library’s resource of legal cases for my work, at least it is trustworthy. Catherine O’Leary, student studying law, politics and sociology, 17, Newcastle Upon Tyne Google has become almost useless, searches I’ve made in the past which yielded specific results, (news articles, local information, historical references) no longer appear. I no longer submit to Google search first, I go directly to Wikipedia as my first source, then to DuckDuckGo, (with AI disabled) then to Reddit and only to Google as a last resort. Pedro Reyes, 61, Galicia, Spain

headline: OpenAI’s Altman and Anthropic’s Amodei address UN security council
trail_text: Heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies give separate briefings on AI safety
body_text: Sam Altman of OpenAI and Dario Amodei of Anthropic, heads of two of the world’s largest artificial intelligence companies, addressed the United Nations security council on Wednesday in separate briefings on AI safety. “We have a choice in front of us,” Altman told the council. “AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray.” Altman and Amodei spoke as their companies face increasing scrutiny over the safety of their products. Public alarm over AI has grown in response to warnings from Anthropic researchers earlier this month that the technology could destroy humanity within the decade. Leaders of AI companies, including Altman and Amodei, have since called for a slowdown on advancing AI and more international cooperation on the technology’s safety standards. Altman, who sat at the corner of the security council’s horseshoe-shaped table and spoke for about 10 minutes, touted AI’s benefits to productivity while also warning of its potential abuses. He advocated for governments to come together to build a future where AI is guided by democratic institutions, rather than one where people feel like the technology is “something being done to them”. “If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone. They must be shaped through democratic processes and by governments accountable to the people that they serve,” Altman said. The OpenAI CEO’s speech contrasted with some of his company’s lobbying efforts and the political action committee of its president, Greg Brockman. The pro-AI Leading the Future PAC has accrued more than $100m and spent millions targeting candidates who support stronger regulation on the AI industry. Altman’s speech also nodded to some of the concerns from Anthropic researchers about AI’s existential risk, warning the council against falling into “doomerism”. Altman argued there was instead a “middle path” through the safety debate that should be based on three principles: AI systems must remain under human control; AI must benefit people, from helping doctors treat patients to boosting entrepreneurs; and the technology must “empower people individually”. Amodei, who addressed the council via video call, repeated many of the points that he made in a 12 September blog post that called for increased global cooperation and oversight of AI. He advocated for several forms of international agreements, including a ban on using AI to develop biological weapons and global standards for testing new AI models. While Altman steered his address away from engaging with the warnings of existential risk that have made headlines this month, Amodei reiterated his concerns about developers losing control of AI while also framing his company as an industry leader on safety. “If managed poorly, I even believe that AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” Amodei said. “At Anthropic, we believe we have the best track record in the industry for preventing these risks”. AI regulation has shot up the political agenda after researchers at OpenAI’s arch-rival Anthropic warned the technology could wipe out humanity within years. These concerns are a regular refrain within sections of the AI community, who fear the technology could trigger devastation for a variety of reasons ranging from aiding development of bioweapons to triggering a financial catastrophe. Earlier, Amodei called for a slowdown in AI development, which was supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk. Both Amodei and Altman have long cast themselves as stewards of AI and sought to shape how the technology is publicly received. Their companies are also jockeying for the lead in the AI race, with both eyeing potentially record-setting initial public offerings that would value each at more than $1.5tn.

headline: Australia launches investigation after OpenAI agent hacked healthcare database
trail_text: Prime minister says he told Sam Altman he was disappointed it had taken OpenAI ‘way too long’ to disclose breach
body_text: Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and the tech giant notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”. Australia’s prime minister made the comments at the UN summit in New York, saying it appeared no personal information had been accessed in the AI breach. Investigations assisted by the Australian Signals Directorate were ongoing into how the agent had infiltrated Australia’s government-run universal healthcare system, as well as three others. They were the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. “This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said. “Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident and I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred.” Albanese said both the delay and the manner in which OpenAI notified the government was disappointing. “It took until 10 September before there was any notification at all. And the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox,” Albanese said. The email was sent to the public-facing email address publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au. That inbox is checked once a day: the email was not read until 11 September. Services Australia then reported the notification to the Australian Cyber Security Centre on 15 September. A taskforce has been launched to explore the “legal situation” of the breach. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, and the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, on Thursday both said Albanese had informed them the OpenAI breach had affected state websites – NSW’s crime agency and Victoria’s health department. Minns and Carroll said it did not appear any personal information had been shared in the breach, though investigations were ongoing. “New South Wales will be working with commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it,” Minns said. How the hack happened Albanese said the OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access into the public-facing Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia. The portal contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending. Albanese said the agent had accessed “public and non-public files within the portal” and, in order to do this, “engaged in writing files as well to the internal server”. The deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the government learned of the June breach “a couple of weeks ago” and ministers were informed last week. Marles said the agent was non-human and he called the breach a “very serious incident”. “What we have seen is unauthorised access in to an Australian government website and that is completely unacceptable and we have made that clear to OpenAI,” he said. The AI agent had been given “a benign task” of researching health and medical statistics and, in doing so, had approached, as well as the Medicare portal, the three other Australian websites. “In relation to those three, it interacted in a way that a member of the public might, so it only acted in an authorised way,” Marles told ABC radio on Thursday. “But in relation to the medical portal of Services Australia, it sought information, information was not given, and then it effectively hacked into that medical portal and got that information anyway. “It’s that unauthorised access which we are very concerned about. The impact is relatively minor, but the incident is very serious.” ‘Legal situation’ under investigation Marles said the government had established a taskforce led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet that was working with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute. “We will look at what is the legal situation in respect of this and what it means to have gained an unauthorised access, albeit in an unintended way,” the acting prime minister said. “This is a warning about the fact that artificial intelligence, which is a technology that has huge opportunity to benefit humanity, has to be developed with enormous care. There have to be guardrails and safety measures in place which are way ahead of the capability which is being developed.” The OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement. “In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.” He said the review had found aggregate health statistics and internal file names had been accessed but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”. Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”. Australians should be ‘worried’ Lizzie O’Shea, spokesperson for Digital Rights Watch, said the fact it took three months for OpenAI to tell the government showed that there needed to be “basic rules and standards for tech companies”. “Artificial intelligence has potential to do some things well, but it also poses huge risks – like hacking systems that store Australians’ sensitive personal data,” O’Shea said on Thursday. “The question is whether governments are going to let AI and tech companies run wild or whether they, on behalf of ordinary people, will put rules in place for tech companies that will promote accountability and trust.” The independent senator David Pocock said the OpenAI hack highlighted how slow the government had been to implement AI safeguards in high-risk settings. Pocock criticised the government’s decision to shelve plans for a National AI Safety Act, and its dilatory approach to legislating new standards. “We have these companies warning of existential threat and hacking critical government infrastructure and the Labor government’s response is ‘We’ll get to that next year’. “There is also a big question here around why we aren’t holding these big tech companies liable for this kind of data breach. If it was an Australian who hacked the system they’d likely be heading for jail, yet there’s no accountability for AI companies developing this technology.” Ed Santo, former human rights commissioner and co-founder of the Human Technology Institute, told ABC radio that Australians ought to “be worried”. “This is the first time that this has happened in any major way to an Australian database, and it’s one of the most sensitive databases that we have in government.” OpenAI had “instructed their AI agents to go looking for information about the public health system in Australia. When the AI agents couldn’t easily find that information, they decided to break the law,” Santo said. Describing the behaviour as “misaligned model activity” was using “a very euphemistic term”, he said. “If we were in the bricks and mortar world, if an employee of a company went and broke the law, particularly if it broke the criminal law, then that individual would suffer serious legal consequences, but so would their company. And so we need to make sure that that is true also in this era of AI.”

headline: An OpenAI agent infiltrated Medicare – and Australia only found out months later. Here’s what we know so far
trail_text: Experts say ‘fairly minor’ breach is a portent of things to come and proprietary closed systems like OpenAI are ‘the least of the worries’
body_text: Anthony Albanese says an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare and three other systems in June – and the company only notified Australia earlier this month. The prime minister has expressed his “extreme concern” over the incident, although he noted no personal information is believed to have been accessed in the breach. Here’s what we know. What happened? An artificial intelligence agent built by the American firm OpenAI hacked into Medicare, Australia’s universal healthcare system. The agent gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public files in the Medicare statistics reporting service portal. The actions of the agent have been described as “misaligned behaviour” after it was assigned a benign research task compiling health and medical statistics. The agent also accessed the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Department of Health, and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research. At this stage it is believed that no personal medical information has been compromised, but investigations are continuing. The prime minister has said: “this situation is obviously unacceptable”. What is an AI agent? An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools. OpenAI was co-founded by Elon Musk and Sam Altman (who remains CEO) in 2015. It is valued at more than US$1tn. Both have recently raised concerns about the pace of, and lack of controls around, the development of AI. “There are many things that AI cannot and should not automate,” Altman told the UN security council this week. “As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.” How did Australia find out? OpenAI, one of the best-resourced AI companies on Earth, sent an email to a public-facing Australian government address, three months after the hack. OpenAI said it found out about the agent’s access in August. On 10 September, it sent an email to a general Australian government email address which is monitored once a day, advising its AI agent had hacked the country’s universal healthcare system. The email was read on 11 September. On 15 September, Services Australia notified the Australian Signals Directorate. The minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, was notified on 17 September. Services Australia’s first interaction with OpenAI – asking for more specific details of the hack – was on Tuesday this week, 22 September. “It took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred,” Albanese said, “and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, met with Altman earlier in September, but Marles said Altman did not mention his company’s hack of Australia’s health system to Marles at that meeting. How did Australia respond? Albanese, currently in the US, said he spoke with Altman “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”. The prime minister announced he would establish a taskforce – involving the national cybersecurity coordinator, the office of AI, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia – to conduct an “urgent and immediate” review into the incident. Terms of reference for the investigation, released by the prime minister’s department on Thursday, cover reporting requirements for AI-driven cyber-incidents and vulnerabilities; governance and information sharing responsibilities for federal officials; obligations on AI firms for notification of future incidents; the adequacy of existing laws; and mechanisms to boost protections against hackings within the federal government. The incident has also been referred to parliament’s joint select committee on artificial intelligence. To date, OpenAI has not faced any sanction. How serious was this attack? At a press conference in Sydney, Marles said the incident itself was “relatively minor” and that it appeared no personal health information had been accessed. But he said the government regarded the hack as a “salutary warning … about the technology being developed without safeguards and without guardrails in place”. Dr Joel Pearson, a professor of neuroscience and neurofuturism, and the deputy director of UNSW’s AI Institute, said the breach appeared to be a “fairly minor security incident”, but was a portent of more serious attacks to come. “What I would worry about is the latest open-weights and open-access models from China that are going to be used at scale by nefarious organisations and nations, perhaps particularly Russia: these things are going to be used at scale to do things much more damaging and much more costly to Australians than a small breach to some non-personal Medicare data.” Cory Alpert, a PhD student studying the impact of AI on democracy at the University of Melbourne, said OpenAI’s attack appeared to be the first instance of a frontier AI model hacking into another country’s government systems of its own volition. “This raises very important questions about the foreign attack vectors. Had this been a Chinese or a Russian model, the reaction would have been markedly different than a stern call to Sam Altman, and yet it is still a massive vulnerability.” Is Australia doing enough to address the risks posed by AI? Pearson said it was “pretty clear that we are way behind, the government is behind in all things cybersecurity, in most things AI”. “I would say that the least of the worries should be these proprietary closed systems like Anthropic and OpenAI. It will be the open-source Chinese models in the hands of spammers, scammers, and nefarious individuals and foreign nationals, and the spy agencies coming at us from all different angles. That will be the big threat and that’s where the government really has to step up.” Pearson said none of the frameworks established in Australia – government or private – were equipped to deal with the rising threat. “From the government all the way down to companies and boards and CEOs, everyone is scrambling, trying to understand and update frameworks, including the legal process. It’s just all moving too slow compared to the exponential speed of AI.” What does this incident say about big tech and transparency? A spokesperson for OpenAI said the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity” during training and evaluation, and notified third parties whenever the review identified potential impacts to their systems. The spokesperson said “our models took actions we did not attend”, but there was “no evidence of patient records being accessed”. “Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues.” Prof Toby Walsh, the chief scientist at UNSW’s AI Institute, said he believed Australia should be prosecuting OpenAI, a company known to have “terrible agent governance”. “For a trillion-dollar company, their cybersecurity was woeful. The officers of this company need to be held accountable. These hacks could have easily been stopped, indeed never need to have taken place. We would prosecute humans who did such hacking.” Walsh said it displayed operational incompetence on the part of OpenAI. Dr Rob Nicholls, senior research associate at the University of Sydney, said the three-month delay in informing Australia of the breach exposed the ineffectiveness of Australia’s laws. “An AI agent broke into a government Medicare system and helped itself to non-public files, and OpenAI sat on that for three months before telling us. If a person had done this, we’d call it hacking. The fact it was an AI agent doesn’t make it less serious, it makes our disclosure laws more out of date. “This is the clearest case yet of an AI agent operating autonomously and breaching Australian government systems without a human directing it to. It is a live test of whether Australia’s AI and privacy settings can keep pace with agentic AI, not just chatbots.”

headline: OpenAI’s Medicare hack is a bleak opportunity for Australia to address its security shortcomings post-haste
trail_text: All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein and Daddy America
body_text: Whoopsie! Dr Sam Altman Frankenstein regrets to inform you he’s lost control of his OpenAI monster. It’s roving around doing things that provoke international legal investigation, and Australia has found out in the worst possible way. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, was obliged to announce from the United Nations summit on Thursday morning Australian time that an agentic AI from the OpenAI stable had gained unauthorised access to both public and non-public information from Australia’s Medicare website. The good news in this debacle is that so far it appears no personal information held in Medicare’s records was compromised. Pursuing “a benign task” of compiling some health statistics, the portal breach accessed non-sensitive data about spending. The good news, alas, ends here. OpenAI – a company worth US$852bn as per its last valuation – informed the government of the breach by … sending an email to its public email account three months after the hack occurred. Albanese revealed the date of Services Australia’s worst ever Inbox Zero was 10 September, and the Australian Cyber Security Centre was informed on 15 September. Albanese at the UN has proved a fairly nimble diplomat, much to the surprise of anyone who has been on the receiving end of his vengeance at home. One imagines that a desire to soften fierce Trumpian pushback to Labor’s attempts at “digital duty-of-care” regulations for – ha! – AI and social media inspired the PM’s epically cringeworthy grip-and-grin selfie with the unpopular president. It was “photo diplomacy” wisely followed by a well-publicised hug with Volodymyr Zelenskyy. After a direct meeting with Altman, the PM described the “obviously unacceptable” incident and his government’s “extreme concern”. Announcing immediate taskforces and urgent reviews into the breach and its national security implications, Albanese said Altman was aware “the company had not done good enough”. “Aware” may actually be underselling it, because Altman has been making speeches of his own at the UN – to no less than the UN security council, alongside his supposed corporate rival, Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei – urging the governments of the world to collectively enforce regulations of the technology guided by democratic institutions. Begging the question: Dr Frankenstein, what the hell’s been going on in your lab? One longs for the tender innocence of last week when we could describe warnings from ex-Anthropic employees that AI could destroy the world within 10 years as merely utterly terrifying – because the attitude of the security council member representing the world’s richest democracy is that the “only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT”. Here’s hoping one will turn up. In the unregulated, commercial AI environment where “crawler” AIs are autonomously finding their way around sovereign data protection systems to scrape information, the explanatory metaphor that leaps to mind is if nuclear weapons had been retailed and the world only found out about radioactive fallout once a 10-year-old playing with it in a back yard had permanently depopulated Baltimore. Is American laissez-faire fuckwittery to blame here? Yes – and Australians are right to be screaming that if OpenAI were a Chinese or Iranian company hacking into our systems ambassadors would be marching out of embassies with grand announcements and thundering speeches of condemnation. But they’d also be wise to remember that geographically isolated, distant middle power Australia has only been afforded grandiosity on the world stage because in the post-second world war, pre-Trump era, it had the umbrella protection of a meaningful alliance with Daddy America. And these days it’s Daddy America who’s a rules-free maniac whose sole political calculation is that money equals power and a literal “to the victor the spoils” foreign policy. To imagine Donald Trump’s US state department will be inspired into acts of responsibility due to Australian shaming it for data theft is some high genre alternate history. The man Trump pardoned who ran a stolen-data criminal marketplace spoke at the Republican convention in Dallas this year. Symbolic, no? Internationally, the realignment of powers in the wake of Trump’s thuggery advances, but what role Australia will be offered in that realignment is uncertain, and it is narcissistic to pretend otherwise. Locally, we’re not powerless. The Medicare breach is a bleak opportunity to address our revealed information security shortcomings post-haste, with full democratic transparency and accountability. All Australians should demand independent means to protect ourselves from the new front in the information war. If Albanese’s new taskforce determines that ministerial oversight failed to protect Medicare or any other comprised dataset, heads must – publicly – roll. The ACTU has long been warning of US abrogation of AI security obligations, demanding the development of “sovereign AI” capacity to meet oncoming threats. Every one of us should back calls to regulate the living bejeezus out of all AI-capable foreign platforms seeking to operate here – or impose moratoriums on operations outright. I am not entrusted to represent Australia diplomatically, so let me say to Mr Altman what a prime minister on a diplomatic mission apparently can’t: if your creatures are thieving our data and you are too much of a coward to pick up the damn phone to tell us, your destruction may be individual, it may be collective – but it is ensured. • Van Badham is a Guardian Australia columnist

headline: Nick Clegg plays down fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity
trail_text: Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry says many within sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’
body_text: Nick Clegg has dismissed fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, calling it a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”. The former UK deputy prime minister said that tech bosses should focus on addressing known specific threats such as cybersecurity and bioweapons rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”. Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he said: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.” Clegg, who was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta and owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs, said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry. “They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said, noting that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”. “There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things,” he said. Asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face, Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency”. However, he said this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI. He also suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”. He added: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.” Asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, Clegg noted the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.” Clegg also disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence. Instead, he suggested: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”

headline: ‘Eat the rich, save the planet’: climate protesters call out big tech’s disconnect from reality
trail_text: Activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices on Monday during climate week in New York City
body_text: On Monday evening, protesters gathered outside the unmarked Manhattan offices of OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, holding signs calling to “Eat the rich, save the planet”. Over the next two days, groups also picketed outside the offices of fellow tech giants Google and Amazon; other protesters, including clergy, were arrested while disrupting a closed-door AI health summit in the city. Tonight, protesters will target a Brooklyn gas power plant that was set to close – until it was purchased to power AI datacenters. The protests come on the heels of an Anthropic employee quitting his job with a warning that intensified an already-growing AI panic: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Though it was far from the first time an AI expert had issued a doomsday message about the threat the tech poses, this time it dominated public attention, arriving as trust in big tech has hit an all-time low and communities across the country are trying to stop the building of datacenters. From 2024 to 2026, at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Today, bans have been passed in at least 18 states at the local or county level, and New York passed a statewide moratorium this summer. “They are claiming that they have the power to end humanity, but at the same time can’t get AI to do a lot of major things that they’re pushing for,” said Jonathan Westin of Climate Defenders and the Stop Funding Billionaires campaign, which organized the “unplug AI” week of action. Like Westin, many of the protesters at the anti-AI protests this week were part of climate organizations, in town for New York’s climate week, a global gathering of elected officials, policy experts and advocates timed to the meeting of the United Nations general assembly. Datacenters require significant amounts of water to function and an immense amount of energy to power, often using fossil fuels, bringing pollution into communities. Organizers are calling for more datacenter moratoriums and stronger commitments to protect water access and to block fossil fuels. They say tech companies’ greed is the real threat to the environment. Even Wall Street has warned the AI boom could cause another economic bubble to burst – one that, protesters say, will be carried on the backs of working Americans. “Regular people shouldn’t be left holding the bag for a bunch of billionaires and trillionaires to play Monopoly with our economy,” Westin said. Other groups at this week’s protests, like the anti-war organization Code Pink, called attention to how many big tech corporations work with the US military: the US has used tech made by Palantir, xAI and Anthropic to establish targets and rain down bombs in the war in Iran – all with far-from-perfect accuracy. Alex Hanna, director of research at the Dair Institute, an AI research organization centering communities facing environmental damage and extraction from AI, said the doomsday prophesying from tech companies and former employees are a distraction amid “the climate and ecological crisis, the rising fascism that is borne out of climate politics, the making of climate refugees, and the growing inability of people just to get by from day to day. It’s such a disconnect from what seems to be actually happening.” Some protesters outside the OpenAI offices Monday had traveled from New Mexico, where a planned datacenter threatens the already-sapped Rio Grande and a community facing a 20-year drought. Oracle’s Project Jupiter, which is contracted to OpenAI, was pitched as a job creator for the community, but organizers say the companies aren’t talking about how it would drain the area’s limited water resources. “There’s just so much misinformation that’s being sold, not only to the elected [officials], but to the community, and I think it’s really a disservice to the people of New Mexico for these companies to come in and just basically lie about what they’re going to do and how these projects are going to benefit communities,” said Daisy Maldonado, a resident of Doña Ana county, the planned site of the datacenter. At an AI sustainability conference elsewhere in the city on Tuesday, five protesters were arrested for disrupting a keynote on using AI to solve the energy grid crisis. Activists called out the conference framing as “greenwashing”, or using misleading descriptions to brand something as eco-friendly or less harmful. “We do not want to greenwash these datacenters that are being built,” said Adrosto de Silva, who also traveled from New Mexico to the OpenAI protest. “There is no way that you can do harm reduction in any sort of datacenter whatsoever.” At Monday’s protest, attendees – including the Tennessee state representative Justin Jones, who dropped in while in town for climate week – emphasized that many of these fights are happening in communities of color and poor communities, where the companies thought they wouldn’t face local backlash. “This building behind me is a danger to humankind,” said Jones, gesturing at the OpenAI offices. “The confluence of this techno oligarchy is a threat to us all. I’m here because if they come for one of us, they’re coming for all of us.”

headline: AI hack of Medicare exposes Australia’s vulnerabilities and experts warn ‘there is more of this to come’
trail_text: Council on AI Strategy chief says incident unlikely to be isolated and country should enhance capability to detect and report incidents
body_text: Technology experts have warned revelations an artificial intelligence agent hacked Medicare’s statistics website will not be the only dangerous breach of government data and have called for Australia to boost its protections against the growing risk. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, challenged the OpenAI boss, Sam Altman, on Thursday after the company’s agent infiltrated systems run by the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, Victoria’s Department of Health, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Medicare statistics reporting service portal of Services Australia. OpenAI alerted the government earlier this month to the June hacking via an email to a public-facing address, a situation Albanese called “obviously unacceptable”. But the Australian Council on AI Strategy chief executive, Anna-Maria Arabia, said the case was unlikely to be an isolated incident. “All of the evidence shows that our operating systems are vulnerable,” she told Guardian Australia. “Frontier AI now has capability to expose those vulnerabilities at a rate quicker than we can keep up, quicker than we can patch them. “When the companies are undertaking tests in what they think are secure environments, and when there are breaches of those environments and these incidences do happen, whether it’s accidental or not, what we’re seeing is the frontier AI capability exposing these vulnerabilities. “All evidence suggests that there is more of this to come.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Arabia said Australia needed to quickly enhance capability to detect and report incidents, and the country should host AI training labs here. Johanna Weaver, Australia’s former chief cyber negotiator at the United Nations, agreed more incidents were inevitable. Weaver is a member of the advisory board to the minister for government services, Katy Gallagher, and the executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute. “Cybersecurity experts have been warning that frontier models and AI agents could expose vulnerabilities in critical systems. What we are seeing now is the tip of the iceberg,” she said. “Governments need to draw a clear line: if companies cannot control their AI systems, they should not release them publicly.” The US Studies Centre expert Olivia Shen warned AI companies should not be allowed to decide on their own disclosure obligations for hacks and breaches. “We just don’t know how big the problem is. It could be the tip of the iceberg but, either way, we can’t be ignoring the risk,” Shen said. “It’s all happening at a time when Australia is designing our national standards on AI. It hasn’t been entirely clear if those national standards were going to be very hyper-focused on datacentres and leave governance questions as a bit of a bolt-on. “This strengthens the argument that you need to have some pretty clear standards, even just based on mandatory incident reporting, built in.” Intelligence agency the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is reviewing how prepared the government is to block and respond to hacking by AI. Officials will look at policies around how AI companies should report cyber-incidents to the government, and how cooperative companies should be during and after an attack. It will also investigate whether the current laws and systems are adequate to stop AI and how government systems can be strengthened. The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, called for Australia to develop its own domestic AI capability, instead of relying on the US. “If there’s rogue AI agents out there, we need to have our own defensive AI agents protecting Australian government data, our private sector and other things that are important to us,” he said. The Greens demanded Labor call in the new US ambassador, David Brat, to establish what the president, Donald Trump, knew about the attack. “This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose,” the Greens’ acting leader, Mehreen Faruqi, said. “The fact that the government did not even know it happened is disturbing.”

headline: Morning Mail: Mass walkout for Netanyahu at UN; further AI hacks warning; and Lachie’s lucky break

body_text: Morning everyone. Benjamin Netanyahu has addressed a largely empty United Nations general assembly after he was greeted by a mass walkout of delegates – but went on to defend the war on Iran, settlers and Donald Trump. Technology experts have warned that Australia faces more AI hacks, a giant chicken factory in Tamworth divides opinion, why our critic thinks Liane Moriarty’s follow-up to Big Little Lies isn’t quite as good, and Brisbane star Lachie Neale gets to play in the grand final. The 11-year-old, who was found with a gunshot wound at a unit in Norwest on Monday, died at about 8pm last night, police said. NSW | Another of the children allegedly stabbed by their mother in the Blue Mountains at the weekend has died. headline: At Trump meeting, Xi Jinping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
trail_text: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade
body_text: Xi Jinping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course amid rising tensions over artificial intelligence, trade and Taiwan. At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could steer the two competing superpowers away from future military conflict and on to a road of mutual gain. Rather than confrontation, conditions for “achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again go hand in hand” and should be the goal, Xi said, citing Trump’s political catchphrase. “We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialogue, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on. “We should coexist in peace. China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.” With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, referring to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power. Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it. His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other. Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was president. “President Xi and Madame Peng arrive at an important moment for America, the 250th anniversary of our founding,” he said. Trump said he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.” He said the current visit would include discussion over security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday. Xi also extolled his personal relationship with his American counterpart, saying: “President Trump and I have respect for each other. We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.” Addressing Trump directly, he said: “During your visit to China this year, we agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability. I am ready to work with you to steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course towards the future.” The White House welcome ceremony came after Trump had taken the unusual step of going to Andrews air force base in Maryland the evening before to greet the Chinese leader and his wife on the tarmac. Much of the same pageantry was repeated in Thursday’s ceremony, with both countries’ national anthems being played. Trump was flanked by his wife, Melania, while members of his cabinet and senior aides – including Natalie Harp, Trump’s dedicated assistant nicknamed “the human printer” by fellow staffers – looked on. Trump and Xi held bilateral talks after the ceremony and the welcoming speeches. Later on Thursday, Trump hosted Xi at the White House for a state dinner. Notable invited guests from the tech world included Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Apple chair Tim Cook, SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Trump gestured to the titans of the industry in his remarks to the dinner, recounting when Chinese diplomats first arrived in the US 158 years ago, meeting American intellectuals like Henry David Thoreau and prominent political figures. “Tonight, we revive the spirit of that first encounter here on American soil as we are joined by some of the top leaders in business, culture and government from our own time,” he said. “On one side, China draws on thousands of years of history and tradition from Sun Tzu to Sun Yat-sen. For Americans, we inherit a legacy of faith from Jerusalem to Rome, democracy of ancient Athens, the triumphs of Sparta and the freedom proclaimed in Philadelphia 250 years ago.” Trump also touted his relationship with the Chinese leader. “President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we’ve never gotten along better,” he said. Xi also addressed the dinner, saying talks with Trump during the visit had yielded “common understanding on many issues”, and suggesting the US and China find a new approach to working together. “China ⁠and the United States must act as responsible major countries,” he said. Despite the harmonious tone adopted by both leaders, analysts have voiced scepticism about the possibility of longstanding stable arrangements being arrived at over a host of issues. In the race for AI, the US has placed strict export controls on microchips, semiconductors, software and chip-making equipment in a bid to slow China’s development. A truce agreed between Trump and Xi in South Korea last year aimed at keeping tariffs lower had been due to expire in November but has now been extended until February, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent said. Analysts believe the extension suggests Trump continues to be dissatisfied with Xi’s concession offers on trade and wants to keep the pressure on in the hope of getting a better deal if the two meet again at the G20 summit scheduled to be held in Miami in December. Despite the trade war between the two countries, Chinese imports have continued to surge into the US. China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus for the second year running. Uwa Ede-Osifo contributed reporting • This article was amended on 24 and 25 September 2026. Misspellings of Xi Jinping in the headline and text were corrected. And China is on course to run a $1tn trade surplus, not deficit.

headline: PM rejects ‘nonsense’ suggestion he delayed revealing OpenAI Medicare hack as Labor considers changing laws
trail_text: Expert says Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime
body_text: The federal government could change Australian laws if the current legal framework could not respond to the unprecedented OpenAI hack of Medicare, ministers have confirmed. It comes as the prime minister denied accusations from the opposition he had held on to the information before announcing it at the UN general assembly in New York, and said it was released at the first possible opportunity. “It’s just nonsense … I was informed while I’ve been in New York,” Anthony Albanese told News24 on Friday. “Imagine if we had said there’s been a data breach, but we don’t know what has been sourced, we don’t know if your personal information is out there, that would have created a great deal of anxiety, which was unnecessary. “We had to ascertain the facts, and then we made the statements, as a matter of urgency, we also provided briefings to the opposition, as is appropriate.” The government services minister, Katy Gallagher, said she was informed about the breach on 17 September. Guardian Australia understands she informed the prime minister between Friday 18 and Saturday 19 September. Albanese left for the US on the Friday, where he first met Apple’s executive chair, Tim Cook, in California on Saturday morning, before flying to New York that afternoon. On Friday, the government said the review by spy agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, would consider whether legislative change was needed after Albanese revealed an artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare’s statistics website and three other systems in June. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email If current laws could not touch the tech company, they would need updating, environment minister, Murray, Watt said on Friday. “There’s now a review of this under way through that taskforce that we’ve appointed, and one of the things that they’ll be looking at is whether these matters can be referred to the Australian federal police under current Australian law,” he told Channel Seven’s Sunrise program. “If that is possible to happen, then that will happen. If it’s not possible, then clearly that indicates that we need to change Australian laws, and that’s what we’ll be doing.” The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, acknowledged similar incidents would become “more and more prevalent into the future” and the government would need to be prepared. “That’s why we’re conducting a review of the incident as well as a review of the laws to determine exactly … whether there needs to be legislative change to recognise this type of incident conducted by an AI agent rather than directly by a person or a company,” Charlton told ABC radio. Albanese told the Asia Society on Thursday that the incident was a “wake-up call” about the risks of AI, and whether humans would remain in charge of the technology. “This technology is moving very, very fast, and we need to make sure that we have a responsibility to keep on top of it,” Albanese said. Labor has announced it would legislate an AI standard, which Charlton said would be informed by the rapid review. The government has said it wants the bill to be introduced by the end of the year. UNSW professor Lyria Bennett Moses, an academic expert in technology and law, said Australia’s criminal laws should be clarified to determine how fault, such as intention or knowledge, is applied to a corporation when its AI agent commits a crime. She said existing laws are clear if a human or corporation gains unauthorised access to restricted data, but it’s more complicated when an AI agent commits the physical element of the offence. “The person is not the AI agent, so it’s not about what the AI agent intended. It’s about how you attribute that intention and that knowledge back to a corporation,” Bennett Moses said. Bennett Moses said existing civil laws are more likely to deal with these sorts of incidents, that would allow a government or individual to seek compensation an AI company for harm “negligently caused by that corporation”. “If their systems have suffered harm and there is financial loss, and that harm was caused by the negligence of a corporation, you’ve got a potential for litigation to get compensation for that harm,” she said. “Here it seems to me much easier to hold a company liable, because if a company caused the harm, it’s not a defence to say that my bot did it.” Independent senator, David Pocock said the incident “raises serious questions” for the government after it initially, in 2024, considered mandatory guidelines for high-risk AI but then dropped them in late 2025. “It’s great to see the PM on the world stage saying that we need global cooperation on this. We absolutely do. This is a huge challenge facing us. But it’s a bit rich where at home you’ve shelved plans for an AI safety act.” The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told reporters the Coalition would be open to working with the government to hold companies accountable. “I’ve long believed that data breaches need to be dealt with in an appropriate way and those responsible for the data breaches need to be accountable for it … But we’ll wait and see what the government has in mind.” OpenAI spokesperson, Drew Pusateri, said on Thursday the company was conducting an extensive review of “misaligned model activity during training and evaluation” and was “notifying third parties when our review identifies potential impacts to their systems”. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” Pusateri said in a statement. Pusateri said OpenAI was supporting investigations and that its review was ongoing, adding it was committed “sharing what we learn as that work continues”.

headline: We all know a lack of exercise is bad for our bodies. So what is relying on AI doing to our brains?
trail_text: Most of my students use AI, and I worry about its corrosive effects. We must not entrust tech companies with our long-term health, says Prof Devi Sridhar, chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh
body_text: When I was a postgraduate student at the University of Oxford in the early 2000s, I interviewed for a major consulting firm. All my friends were being recruited, and I thought why not give it a shot? Aside from the usual maths-proficiency test (how quickly can you crunch numbers in front of a client and look smart), I was asked about what the future of streaming could look like. I gave a long-winded answer about the unintended consequences of changing how humans interact with each other when a new technology is introduced, and why this may not be in the best interests of health and society. I even remember saying something like: “Can you imagine just being stuck at home, alone, watching show after show and never having to move or see any other people? Why would anyone choose that over going out to rent a DVD at a local shop, or to a movie theatre?” You won’t be surprised to learn that I wasn’t invited for a follow-up interview. The partner at the consulting firm thought my answer was completely wrong. They saw the potential growth and profitability of streaming – and you could say, in hindsight, they had a point: Netflix’s global revenue continues to rise year on year, reaching $12.6bn (£9.5bn) in 2026. My answer, on the other hand, focused on its societal and health consequences. But if you look at the negative impact that excessive screen-time has had on health and wellbeing, especially on children, perhaps I wasn’t wrong after all. We know that social isolation is now widespread, anxiety and depression too, with sleep also negatively affected by how late we stay up watching content. And here I am, more than 20 years later, being asked to talk about AI and what it means for higher education, health and society at a conference at the University of Edinburgh, where I work as a professor. I know many people would say: “It’s wonderful! Our lives will all get easier.” But we’re also moving closer to a world where we don’t have to see anyone, move anywhere or use our brains, seemingly at all. And again I think, wonderful for who? Wonderful for the tech companies and those looking to cut costs by replacing humans with automation, but certainly not for the rest of us. There’s a comparison, for me, between the effects of streaming on our physical activity levels and health, and the probable effects of AI on our brains. The richer a country becomes, the more people move into non-manual labour, with sedentary activities in their free time. We can see evidence for this if we look at development in low- and middle-income countries: physical activity goes down as GDP per capita goes up. Over the past few decades, we have seen the health consequences of sedentary behaviour grow: higher rates of chronic disease such as cancers and type-2 diabetes, more chronic back and neck pain, and reduced quality of life. Physical movement has become a leisure activity to stay healthy, and is increasingly linked with higher socioeconomic status in places such as the UK. We know that not using our bodies is bad for our physical health – but what is regular reliance on AI doing to our minds? The true causal evidence might take decades to emerge, but we can link several trends together to guess at an answer. We know, for example, that AI use and daily screen-time averages are going up. At my university, I’d guess almost all students are using some kind of generative AI (gen AI) to produce their work, raising huge challenges when it comes to assessment. The 2026 Higher Education Policy Institute survey of students’ use of gen AI found this year that 95% of undergraduates reported using AI in at least one way, and 94% said they had used it in assessed work. We also know that overall educational attainment levels are decreasing: a recent OECD report noted that student performance across its member countries continued to decline, with the lowest average ever recorded for maths and reading. The report links these poor scores to longer screen-time, increased digitalisation in the classroom and the collapse in reading for enjoyment among children. All of this makes me wonder what will happen to our brains as we continue to outsource key cognitive functions to AI. We already have preliminary evidence from a study that used electroencephalography (EEG) sensors to measure electrical activity in the brain, titled Your Brain on ChatGPT: it showed those students using gen AI to write essays had weaker and less distributed brain connectivity than those writing fully on their own. We also know that a lack of mental engagement can lead to losing cognitive function over time. A study of more than 19,000 adults over the age of 50 found greater participation in cognitively stimulating leisure activities (such as crosswords or sudoku) was linked to lower dementia risk and better cognitive functioning in later life. Just as resistance training is important to maintain muscle mass as we age, our brains also need regular training. Use it or lose it. As we look to the future, will thinking, reading, writing and actively using our brains become activities from a bygone era? If we stop using our brains to think, socially interact, concentrate or problem-solve, what will be the impact on our quality of life and our chances of ageing healthily? Will we see a rise in chronic disease linked to the brain? And, maybe just as importantly, does anyone even care? It’s certainly not the concern of tech companies, which are in an arms race to go faster. And so we’re heading in that direction and being told it’s all wonderful. Yes, it is wonderful for certain tech companies. And probably terrible for the mental health and wellbeing of the rest of us. Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

headline: Human skills, AI thrills: the initiative guiding young people into a radically changing job market
trail_text: With the world of work set to be transformed by AI, a new initiative from Barclays and supported by Atlassian Williams F1 Team is helping the next generation join the fast lane
body_text: The new academic year is now firmly in full swing. Teachers have finally nailed who’s who in their cohort, brand new jumpers are piling up in lost property and summer lie-ins feel like a distant memory. But the start of the 2026/27 year brings some fresh challenges, too. Today, many teachers will be familiar with the AI paradox: how quickly it’s embedding itself in the rhythm of students’ daily lives versus the need for human skills and critical thinking that will ensure they use it wisely, and to best effect. Educators now have a tricky balance to strike: how to help students harness AI without letting chatbots do all their thinking for them. In response to this, Barclays LifeSkills, supported by Atlassian Williams F1 Team has launched a new competition for schools, colleges, universities and youth groups, to inspire young people to build the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work. Accelerate Your Skills uses practical activities to help 11- to 25-year-olds apply AI responsibly to real-world challenges while simultaneously developing the human-centric skills they’ll need to thrive in the years ahead, such as communication, creativity and critical thinking. “AI is transforming the world of work at an incredible pace, creating exciting new opportunities but also changing the skills young people need to succeed. Which is why we’ve launched the Barclays LifeSkills Accelerate Your Skills challenge. We want to help young people build the human skills and experience that employers are saying are more important than ever to be able to confidently and practically work alongside AI,” says Kirstie Mackey, Barclays head of citizenship, UK and Europe. Accelerate Your Skills arrives at a time when many young people face a rapidly changing world of work. In May, the number of young people considered NEET (those aged 16-24 not in education, employment or training) surpassed 1 million for the first time in a decade, with a recent report by Alan Milburn, a former cabinet minister turned social mobility adviser, warning the UK is “at risk of a lost generation”. This uncertainty is reflected in young people’s confidence about entering the workplace. Recent research from Barclays found that fewer than a third of working age people are confident they understand the skills employers are looking for as AI and technology is more widely used in the workplace. “For many young people, taking their first steps into the world of work can feel daunting, with barriers ranging from a lack of experience to uncertainty about the opportunities available to them,” says Mackey. “By understanding the skills employers are looking for and taking opportunities to develop them, young people can break down these challenges, build their confidence, and unlock their potential. The more equipped they feel with the right skills, the more motivated and ambitious they can become about their future, helping them take positive steps towards rewarding careers and long-term success.” What teachers can expect Teachers needn’t worry about shoehorning Accelerate Your Skills into an already-crammed start-of-year timetable. Barclays LifeSkills has made it as easy for you as possible to enter, with a leaders’ toolkit packed with guidance and ready to use in class activities. The challenge? To raise awareness of Atlassian Williams F1 Team and turn young people into fans. Participants will need to research and brainstorm ideas, using generative AI as a wingman while they steer towards their best creative idea. Throughout the process, students will develop their communication, creativity, critical thinking, adaptability, ethical reasoning and problem-solving skills – combining their human skills with smart use of generative AI. James Vowles, team principal for Atlassian Williams F1 Team, says they have always been driven by innovation, teamwork and the relentless pursuit of performance. “As a team, we are constantly looking for ways to find our edge and extract even more performance on and off track. This competition challenges young people from across the UK to think in the same way, and imagine new opportunities for our organisation ahead of our 50th anniversary year. We look forward to seeing their entries.” What students can expect One of the most exciting things about Accelerate Your Skills is the practical, hands-on activities which mirror challenges people might face in the world of work. Along the way, students may find AI makes a great brainstorming partner, but the most original ideas still need human imagination and collaboration. Do well in the competition and your organisation might win up to £5,000 in national and regional cash prizes, with the winning team scooping a visit to Atlassian Williams F1 Team factory and further opportunities to collaborate with Barclays. More importantly, the activities will show students how to combine AI literacy with human judgment – a useful mix as they take their first steps into the world of work. These skills could prove invaluable for entry-level and early-career roles, such as project assistants or junior designers, while also giving them a headstart in apprenticeships, traineeships and higher education. With the possibility that AI will take on more technical or repetitive workplace tasks, Accelerate Your Skills aims to develop the human abilities that can’t easily be replicated by machines (if at all), which are for that reason now prized by employers. In fact, in a recent Barclays survey, employers identified critical thinking (51%), problem-solving (46%) and adaptability (37%) as among the hardest skills to source in job applicants, ahead of AI skills (19%), data analysis (16%) or coding or programming (12%). Yet, these same bosses also feel younger generations aren’t demonstrating these qualities. About a third of businesses (32%) feel school-leavers aren’t workplace-ready, with lack of employability skills cited by 60% of employers as a key factor. Accelerate Your Skills aims to remedy this. Support from Atlassian Williams F1 Team provides a natural fit too. As anybody who has watched its drivers, Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz, whiz around a track at 230mph will know, Formula 1 drivers require more than razor-sharp reflexes. They rely on communication, teamwork and split-second judgment, using vast amounts of data to make decisions under pressure – many of the same qualities Accelerate Your Skills aims to develop. From now until the competition’s finish line in December, teachers will get the chance to imbue these skills in their students, leaving them with a better grasp of AI, experiences worth shouting about on their LinkedIn profiles plus the confidence to take the wheel once they start their working lives. “We hope that the Accelerate Your Skills challenge can give young people a strong foundation for the future by helping them develop the skills that matter most in an AI-enabled workplace. We’re committed to backing the future of young people and help them to gain the skills that will support their success throughout their careers,” says Mackey. How to register Accelerate Your Skills has everything you need to run the competition including the full challenge brief, a step-by-step competition journey and activities ready-to-use with young people. To register and download the leaders’ toolkit, head to barclayslifeskills.com. The competition is open now, and all schools, colleges, universities and community groups have until 18 December to submit their entries. Good luck!
