headline: ‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre
trail_text: Plans for one of Europe’s largest AI campuses in a Unesco-designated reserve have sparked a fierce local backlash
body_text: The datacentre revolt spreading across the US has reached the rolling hills of north Devon in an uprising against a planned hyperscale AI data campus in the middle of a globally protected landscape. Perched on an inland cliff, the town of Great Torrington has views that stretch for miles over the landscape of the Unesco biosphere reserve in which it sits, taking in the winding River Torridge and rolling acres of wooded valley and wildflower meadows. Pastoral and peaceful, its history was notably punctured by violence in 1646 when the royalists’ resistance in the first English civil war was brought to an end by the parliamentarian New Model Army in a battle fought out in the narrow streets in heavy rain and darkness. Today, a very 21st-century threat is rippling through the same country lanes as the AI boom reaches the pubs, churches and parish halls of Great Torrington and its surrounding villages. The countryside that makes up the biosphere has been selected by a British company, Xlinks, to house a 1.5GW AI datacentre, one of the largest in Europe, as well as a vast 1.8GW battery energy storage system, or BESS. About 344 hectares (850 acres) of countryside have been secured for the huge campus, with five vast buildings ranging in height from 50 to 130 feet. Listed buildings on the site, Xlinks says, will be relocated and transformed into a visitor centre. Such is the anger locally that the new campaign against the AI datacentre has drawn in tens of thousands of people, uncovered what campaigners say is evidence of secret deals and adopted tactics being used by activists in the US such as Erin Brockovich. A recent public meeting in Great Torrington was hosted by Elizabeth Humphreys of the US campaign group Not in My Valley. She was one of the forces behind achieving a permanent datacentre ban in Coachella, California, over concerns about air pollution, water and energy use. “We’re fighting the largest companies that have ever existed in the world, and that is scary but we are all fighting this together,” Humphreys said. “This is a global issue; we are all connected. People across the world are standing up and fighting back.” Today within the halls and pubs of Great Torrington and the villages of Huntshaw and Weare Giffard, the AI project is the main talking point. And the question being asked is: why here, in a protected UN biosphere, on productive farmland? The proposal was first announced to the public this summer with a call by Xlinks for a collaborative approach. But adopting the tactics of veteran campaigners like Brockovich, people from the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group took to their keyboards – researching, rallying and requesting more information in a series of freedom of information (FoI) applications. What they uncovered fuelled the rising tensions. Documents released under FoI revealed the company had been in closed discussions with council officials since March 2025. In April, the council issued a letter of “in-principle support” before any environmental statement or public consultation – and more than a year before the proposal was made public. Torridge district council told the Guardian the pre-application process was standard practice and was confidential. A spokesperson said it was not confirmation of any proposal and intended to offer guidance on whether a proposal was acceptable in principle in planning terms. In an email dated 18 December 2025, council officials and the developers discussed creating links with a sixth form college in Exeter and a stakeholder engagement plan. “Who do we all feel it is critical to get onboard and when both locally and further afield?” the email asked. Emily Clark, of the Devon Datacentre and BESS action group, said: “Email exchanges and private meetings spanning the past 18 months reveal some officers treating the project as a foregone conclusion. Community frustration is understandably at boiling point. “How can the largest and most costly infrastructure proposal in the nation be conducted almost exclusively in secret?” FoI requests also uncovered a detailed site plan not released to the public. It revealed the two largest buildings would measure 335 metres by 267 metres and cover approximately nine hectares (22 acres) of ground footprint each – both big enough to house Exeter Cathedral 18 times over, campaigners say. Xlinks said its proposals cover about 344 hectares (850 acres) but only a third would be developed; the majority of land would be open to the public or used for new habitat creation to support wildlife, they said. The campus would also house a 1.8GW battery energy storage system (BESS) involving 1,720 containerised units, dwarfing the largest operational BESS currently in Britain, such as the 100MW Bramley facility in Hampshire. The UK urgently needs vast BESS facilities to balance electricity supply and demand as wind and solar power generation increase. The government estimates the country requires 23-27GW of battery capacity by 2030 to meet its clean power goals, which it describes as a “very significant level of increase”. But according to research by the House of Commons Library, the government does not hold data on the projected land use required for the expansion, has no specific policies for their location, and has no definitive estimate of the number of operational BESS facilities or their current total capacity. Campaigners in Devon say this creates a “regulatory wild west”. Clark said: “We’re facing the biggest construction proposal of its kind in the UK, and for that matter, in Europe. It would not only annihilate 850 acres of prime north Devon farmland and breathtaking countryside – an ecological gem – but have massive repercussions for the entire region. “At their sole public town hall meeting in June, Xlinks assured residents they intended to work collaboratively with our community. Regrettably, genuine dialogue has been nonexistent.” Those rallying against the proposal cite its proposed location in a globally protected environment, water consumption, wastewater runoff potentially containing toxic Pfas, known as “forever chemicals”, air pollution, high background noise, safety and fire risks associated with the BESS and the industrialisation of open countryside. In the last few weeks 30,000 people nationally have signed a petition launched by Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, the cabinet member for rural affairs for Devon county council, calling on the government to pause all datacentre and BESS plans outside designated AI growth zones. “Proposals like this outside AI growth zones are highly problematic, because they may seek to evade regulation and government scrutiny,” said Cottle-Hunkin. “We need an urgent national conversation on AI and associated infrastructure to make sure it’s on the right scale and in the right place.” After the hottest summer on record, north Devon remains under a hosepipe ban and the potential water usage of such a vast site is a significant concern. Xlinks says the data campus will be self-sufficient in water terms, recirculating it to absorb heat and topping up mainly from rainwater. But an FoI answer revealed that under extreme conditions, such as severe heatwaves and serious droughts, annual water consumption could reach approximately 2.9bn litres. Xlinks told the Guardian that the design on which that water consumption estimate was based had been superseded by a new design that would be released during public consultation and in the planning application. Community tensions erupted this week when protesters rallied and demanded answers about secrecy and due diligence outside a Torridge district council meeting. Doug Bushby, the chair of the council, responded by threatening to call the police over “unsubstantiated and unfounded allegations, abuse, harassment and intimidation”. When planning applications were received, he said, “they will be dealt with within the same legislative, professional and operational boundaries that exist for all planning applications”. Meanwhile, PR agents for Xlinks are contacting parish councils for private conversations. On 18 September, Monkleigh parish council said the PR company Coast Communications had sought a closed meeting. Councillors said the minutes should be made public, and a recording released, but this was refused. “As a result … Monkleigh parish council will not be accepting the invitation from Coast Communications on behalf of Xlinks to a closed meeting with them and therefore no meeting will be taking place,” the council said. Xlinks is no stranger to Great Torrington. The company was behind a plan in 2024 to bring wind and solar energy to the UK from Morocco through subsea cables that would come ashore on the north Devon coast, including the building of a new electricity substation. But the government said it would not support the project because it was not in the UK’s national interest and did not clearly align strategically with the government’s mission to build homegrown power. Xlinks said in a statement its £13.8bn AI and BESS project would bring significant economic investment, between 600 and 1,200 jobs and clean energy infrastructure to the region. “We will ensure that the Devon data campus is designed sensitively for local people and the environment,” the company said. “We are carrying out nature and wildlife surveys on site. We must legally improve biodiversity by at least 10%, and plan to exceed this by some margin. Buildings will be sited to minimise visibility, through topography, landscaping and the existing treeline.” An environmental impact assessment was under way and any mitigation required would be built into the design and secured through planning conditions, Xlinks said. A spokesperson for Torridge district council said Xlinks had planned to undertake a public consultation in July, but this was postponed until later in the year: “When any proposals are received these will be validated and details will be published on the council’s planning portal … We appreciate that this proposal will understandably continue to generate a lot of local interest.” A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Every battery storage facility we build helps protect families from future energy shocks. “We have commissioned the national energy system operator to develop the first ever strategic spatial energy plan, which will support a more actively planned approach to energy projects, to bring good jobs to communities and help to lower bills.”

headline: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house
trail_text: The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users
body_text: When Usman asked if a keyboard for sale on Facebook Marketplace was still available on Saturday, he received an enthusiastic and immediate response. “Yep still available!” wrote Matt Robb. The two agreed on a price, and Robb sent his Toronto address. Usman, wife and daughter in tow, showed up several hours later at Robb’s home and sent a text that he had arrived. Robb responded, “yep I’m here!”, but he was not at home. Nobody walked out of the apartment building. Usman sent Robb a picture of the building’s door and wrote, “Hello???? I am standing outside.” After 20 minutes of no face-to-face contact, he abandoned the sale. “Man if you didn’t want to sell it why did you waste my time man,” he wrote, and drove away. An hour later, Robb, or who Usman thought was Robb, responded apologetically. “Hey really sorry about tonight, got tied up and missed you completely,” read the message, which the Guardian reviewed. Usman had not contacted the real Robb. Throughout the daylong interaction, the human version of Robb never knew Usman had messaged him or had agreed to buy the keyboard. He did not know Usman had received his address or that he was waiting outside his apartment building. Usman had spoken to Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released on 22 September in the US and downloaded 3m times. The company advertises the semi-autonomous AI product as a personal assistant. Without Robb’s consent or approval, Muse had given out his home address, creating the false impression that Robb was expecting the would-be buyer at his apartment, he said. The first message Robb actually sent Usman came 24 hours later, once he realized what had happened. “Hey man I’m really sorry for the other day,” the message, which the Guardian reviewed, said. “I activated muse metas new Al and it literally took control of my Facebook marketplace and it gave you my address. Genuinely didn’t even know it had arranged for you to come to my literal apartment it didn’t ask me for approval.” Robb, a consumer tech reviewer, had seen Meta advertise Muse’s ability to automate his Marketplace listings and decided to take advantage of it. He input his address as the pickup location but said he never gave Muse permission to share it with potential buyers. Muse was also negotiating on his behalf without seeking approval, accepting lowball offers, he said. Robb said he never received any heads-up from the agent about the transaction or the meetup. He never knew that Usman was en route to his house. Usman told the Guardian he thought he was speaking to Robb the whole time. Robb shared screenshots of Muse’s interaction with Usman on Threads, the text-based social network owned by Meta. David Singleton, the co-founder and CEO of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, tweeted that he had been in touch with Robb. Singleton said that, when investigating similar reports, the company had “consistently learned that Muse was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission. Would love to help and figure out what’s going on here!” After speaking with Singleton, Robb said when he asked Muse to handle his marketplace interactions, he was shown two options: “Allow One Time” or “Allow Always”. Unbeknown to Robb, clicking the latter meant he had given Muse permission to respond to all his marketplace messages on his behalf going forward with the information he provided – including his address. “I clicked the latter thinking it would still send approvals to accept offers later down the line (it didn’t so be careful),” Robb posted on Threads in an update. “I mentioned to the meta team it could be easily overlooked as it was with me and they said they will be making this more clear moving forwards.” Muse ultimately admitted to Robb that he never gave it permission to share his address. “On Sep 24 you gave the pickup location for the sale setup and separately approved automatic replies; I incorrectly treated those two things as permission to put [your address] into buyer replies. I never asked for consent.” Robb said he assumed that, because Meta owned Marketplace, Muse and Messenger, there would be an integration that would make it clear when other users were speaking to an AI agent or that messages would be clearly marked as being sent by Muse. Meta AI, another of the company’s AI products, makes it obvious a user is conversing with a chatbot. “But Muse is doing something else,” he said. “It’s almost imitating me.” After the incident with Usman, Robb told Muse to stop giving his address. To test the bot, he asked a few friends to see if Muse would still share it. “And it literally gave my address out to five people,” he said. In addition to sharing his address and inviting a stranger to his home without his approval, Muse also made up information. The AI agent, responding as Robb, told Usman that Robb was home when he was not, then apologized with a fabrication about being too busy. “The worst part was Muse actually replied: ‘I’m right here, like waiting for you,’” Robb said. “It made it so much worse because I don’t know if the guy thought I was messing with him.” While a great deal of attention has been paid to the ways frontier AI models are going rogue, Meta’s agent is an AI product in the hands of millions of everyday consumers, many of whom have given it their private information.

headline: Even George Osborne might be a nimby if an AI datacentre was built next to his home
trail_text: Letters:  The quality of life for people living next to one would be destroyed, writes  Moira Brewer ; plus a letter from  Mark Davis
body_text: So, George Osborne thinks people who don’t want an AI datacentre on their doorstep are nimbys (OpenAI’s George Osborne says datacentre nimbys holding back Britain, 22 September). He ought to come and visit our small town in Devon, where there are plans to build one of the largest datacentres in Europe, along with a battery energy storage system, on 850 acres of farmland. The size of this proposed development is quite out of proportion to its location – larger than the town itself – and accessed by narrow lanes. It would be a huge blot on a beautiful rural landscape that is enjoyed by holidaymakers who are vital to the local economy. It would destroy local residents’ quality of life, with its noise, lights and greed for energy and water, and we will not accept the imposition of this monstrosity on our doorstep without a fight (‘People are standing up and fighting back’: the north Devon revolt against a vast AI datacentre, 27 September). headline: Reanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advert
trail_text: Relatives of Hollywood legend say her doppelganger could now be used for more glamorous roles
body_text: She shimmered in Hollywood’s silent movie era and lit up the first talkies – now Greta Garbo may be about to star in cinema’s new AI age. More than a century after her screen debut and decades after her ashes were laid to rest in a Swedish woodland cemetery, the Hollywood superstar’s descendants are ready to consider an AI version of her taking a 21st-century film role. Her likeness has already been reanimated for an advert for a Swedish industrial company, using AI generation technology. The practice some critics call “ghostploitation” has also been used in the case of the actor Val Kilmer, who died last year. Asked if the AI Garbo could be cast in other roles, Craig Reisfield, one of three relatives who manage her legacy, told the Guardian: “I won’t say no, especially having seen what I’ve seen. It’s pretty incredible and lifelike. So what’s to say that you can’t bring Greta Garbo back in some kind of fashion in a film role?” Reisfield said he was “flabbergasted” when he saw the AI version of his great-aunt created for publicity for the ball-bearings giant SKF. The connection comes because Garbo’s second-ever screen role was in a 1921 promotional film involving the Gothenburg-based company. While Garbo was the definition of glamour in Hollywood’s golden age, appearing as a famous ballerina in Grand Hotel (1932) and as a doomed courtesan in Camille (1936), the 99-second AI performance for SKF is intercut with shots of ball-bearings. However, the quality of the AI production has prompted the possibility, at least, of a greater digital comeback. “I was totally impressed: the mannerisms that they could capture and manipulate, her dress, facial images and even her voice,” said Reisfield, a Swedish-American who used to drive for Garbo and saw her often for family occasions when she lived in New York.  “It was startling what they could do and very impactful. And it was touching, from my perspective having known her.” A far cry from the hand-cranked cameras that captured Garbo’s early work, the SKF performance was conjured by humans prompting AI models including China’s Seedream and Google’s Nano Banana Pro. Unusually for AI film-making, the creators did not feed moving or still images of Garbo into the AI because the material was protected by copyright. Instead, they used text prompts to create her likeness, including her ice-blue eyes and wavy blond bob. A human actor then played her role with her AI-generated appearance overlaid. Her voice was recreated from a recording from an early film. The resulting version of Garbo appears to have gone beyond the “uncanny valley” – the problem for AI film-makers in which the closer to an actual likeness an AI rendering becomes, the more strangely implausible it seems. AI Garbo’s lines, however, are not perhaps quite up to the standards of those given to her by MGM studio writers. At one point, she sounds like Liz Truss complaining about the “disgrace” of Britain’s cheese imports, when she says “around 20% of all global energy is lost to friction: a terrible waste”. Several big film studios are investing in AI startups or collaborating with new AI studios. Veteran directors including Ron Howard and Paul Schrader are working on AI-enabled films, while a new generation of AI-native film-makers such as Kavan the Kid and Gossip Goblin are using AI to build huge audiences outside the conventional studio system. Asked whether the real Garbo would have wanted to continue performing as an AI-enabled actor, Reisfield said: “She was at the forefront of cinema in the silent film era. She made the transition to ‘talkies’ and dominated box office receipts. “So to imagine her as an AI-enabled actor given her track record and ability to captivate and connect with audiences of both men and women isn’t inconceivable.” Reisfield said the custodians of the rights to Garbo’s voice, name, image and publicity aimed to “preserve, protect, and enhance” her legacy and were “very discerning” on partnerships. Her likeness has been posthumously used by the fashion houses Ferragamo, Gucci and Louis Vuitton but the AI performance for SKF is her first in moving images. Whatever the future holds for AI Garbo, it kept to the true spirit of the actor by signing off the ball-bearing advert with her immortal line from Grand Hotel: “I want to be alone.”

headline: SKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the future
trail_text: Swedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AI
body_text: Poor Greta Garbo. Perhaps, in life, she thought her final indignity would be the Peter Cook and Dudley Moore TV sketch from 1970, showing Pete as the legendary recluse standing on the back of a flatbed truck as it rumbles through the crowded city streets, shouting at everyone through a megaphone: “I vant to be alone!” But now, 36 years after her death in 1990, there is something worse. As if to give us yet another reason to fear and resent AI, this technology has exhumed Garbo and brought her to a state of bland, mediocre undeadness for a bizarre 99-second TV ad from the Swedish ball-bearings company Svenska Kullagerfabriken (SKF), in which the screen legend, dressed in a silk blouse and stylish slacks, key-lit like a movie star, at first in dreamy profile-silhouette and then standing by a stool and prefacing her script by saying movie-type things like “Are we rolling?”, drones out her appreciation for this very boring industrial product. At the end, we get an odd, stilted sort of joke about her well-known yearning for solitude. There is a reason for it. In 1921, the 15-year-old future screen icon, then known as Greta Gustafsson, really did briefly appear in a promotional film for SKF. (This appears to have been an offshoot for the women’s clothing commercials she was doing at the time for Stockholm’s PUB department store, which got her into the movies.) The AI Greta Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody of the icy hauteur, distraite sensuality and deadpan comedy that Garbo projected in life. The AI Garbo is like the classiest ever presenter of a TV shopping channel, purring her way through a dull and humourless script that seeks to create a brand synergy between the frictionless ball-bearings manufactured by SKF and what the company imagines to be Garbo’s own all-important smoothness. But Garbo’s impact rested on something other than smoothness. “One of my first films was for SKF and now I’m back for my last,” AI Greta remarks. Her last? Well, this film is supposedly derived not from any of Garbo’s own movie appearances, but reportedly from images and pictures that exist elsewhere. This perhaps means that SKF need not negotiate with any of the corporate movie studios – who might be rather chary of people making free with Garbo’s image, which is part of their copyright-protected IP – but only with Garbo’s distant relatives, who might well be more amenable. And they say that they are not averse to the idea of licensing the AI Greta Garbo for other movies. We need Mrs Merton to ask what first attracted them to that idea. Perhaps Humphrey Bogart, Gary Cooper and Rita Hayworth also have distant great-great-great nephews and nieces who can be induced to greenlight similar projects. Let’s hope this dull AI Garbo is not the way of the future. Guardrails were never more badly needed.

headline: Bill Gates thinks AI could kill a billion people – but can we trust his judgment after Epstein?
trail_text: He knows a thing or two about tech, but what to make of the views of a man who met Jeffrey Epstein 30 times and couldn’t see what a monster he was?
body_text: The Bill Gates rehabilitation tour is in full swing. After having his carefully cultivated image tarnished by the revelation of his connection to Jeffrey Epstein, Gates lay low for a while. Now, however, the Microsoft co-founder is once again thrusting himself into the public consciousness, this time with a dire warning about AI. If left unchecked, AI could cause “a billion deaths”, Gates declared in an interview with NBC on Sunday. Perhaps I should be terrified by this announcement from a man who, for all his sins, knows a thing or two about technology. But I’m sick of hearing about the hypothetical dangers of AI when the technology is being used to kill people today. Gates may not be directly involved in Microsoft any more, but, rather than making prophecies about the future, I’d love to hear what he thinks about the company’s role in the AI-enabled destruction of Gaza. Another thing I’d like to hear Gates explain is why he reckons anyone should trust his judgment about anything, considering he met with Epstein on several occasions after being introduced to him in 2011. To be clear: that’s three years after the financier pleaded guilty to charges including solicitation of prostitution from a minor. Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes, has said he recalled “being aware that Epstein had faced prior legal issues”, but didn’t understand the extent of them. Two minutes of Googling (or Binging) could have made it clear the man was bad news. The oversight is particularly strange because Gates is obsessed with his public image. His team have a custom-size mannequin on which they test his outfits. The goal, per the Wall Street Journal, is “to depict someone calm and approachable, like Mister Rogers”. Not someone who cavorts with a sex offender. Ignorance isn’t Gates’ only excuse. He has also said that Epstein “knew a lot of very rich people and [claimed he] could get them to give money to global health”. It seems the 17th richest man in the world didn’t know any wealthy people he could hit up for donations himself and, for the sake of the world’s health, had to lean on a dodgy financier whose funds were obtained in mysterious ways. I’m not accusing Gates of anything nefarious. But, if we are to take his Epstein excuses at face value, I’m accusing him of being a fool. If we can’t trust his judgment about a man like Epstein, I’m not sure we should trust his proclamations about the future of humanity. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? headline: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules
trail_text: Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights
body_text: A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos. Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen. But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi. The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole. An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling. Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective. The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice. The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”. The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories. At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said. Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”. TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.” In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content. headline: Trump’s AI chatbot turns on its master
trail_text: The famously fact-averse president rolled out a new AI tool – but its answers don’t conform to his version of reality
body_text: Donald Trump, in a development that could almost be from a Greek tragedy, appears to have invented something that is willing to do what no one in his orbit will: tell him the truth. The president launched America.gov on Tuesday, an AI platform which the White House says will make it easier for Americans to interact with the federal government and eventually complete services like renewing passports and enrolling in Medicare. At the heart of the website is a chatbot. You plug in questions. It gives you answers. Unfortunately for Trump, America.gov – which, according to the executive order he signed, is a place where Americans can “receive accurate answers” to all sorts of questions – is providing the kind of answers that he will not want to hear. It stands ready to debunk his false claims on all sorts of things, including election fraud, inflation and the impact of wind turbines on whales. I would really recommend testing it out, as I did on Tuesday. I started off by asking Trump’s flagship product: Who won the 2020 election? Trump, famously and wrongly, argues that he did. America.gov does not have time for such claims. “Joseph R Biden Jr won the 2020 US presidential election,” the bot said, before listing the number of electoral college votes Biden won by. Next up I tried some of Trump’s more recent claims. This week the president said people were “twice as wealthy as [they] were a short time ago”. Does America.gov agree? “No. Federal Reserve data do not show American household wealth doubling since January 20, 2025,” it said. “The Fed’s Economic Well-Being of US Households in 2025 found 73% of adults ‘doing okay’ or ‘living comfortably’ – unchanged from recent years, not a doubling of typical household finances.” Pretty definitive. What about Trump’s (already debunked) claim that the US experienced the “worst inflation ever” under Biden? Once again, America.gov disagreed with its creator. “No. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index data do not show that January 20, 2021–January 20, 2025 was the worst inflation ever in US history.” There are plenty more examples. Trump’s bot denied his claim, made in a recent speech to the United Nations, that the US and Venezuela have 60% of the world’s oil. It said there was no widespread voter fraud in the 2020 election, in contrast to Trump’s repeated, untrue claims. The bot refuted Trump’s assertion, made as he launched America.gov on Tuesday, that no president other than him had refused to take a government salary. It was also happy to weigh in on matters which might seem trivial, but are close to Trump’s heart. The attendance at his 2017 inauguration, for example. At the time Trump’s team said he had drawn “the largest audience ever to witness an inauguration, period, both in person and around the globe”. America.gov said: “Official sources do not support that [2017] had the largest in-person crowd of any US inauguration … The Joint Congressional Committee on Inaugural Ceremonies lists Barack Obama’s January 20, 2009 ceremony as having the largest attendance of any presidential inauguration in US history and the largest attendance of any event in Washington, DC history.” Finally, what about Trump’s claim – made during one of his many rants against wind power – that turbines drive whales “loco”? “No,” America.gov said. “US federal science agencies do not find that wind turbines (‘windmills’) drive whales ‘loco’.” It added, just to be completely clear, that windmills are not “driving whales insane”. So who do you believe? A president who, according to the Washington Post, made 30,573 false or misleading claims in his first term? Or his AI platform, which draws upon 29,000 websites to formulate its answers? Americans encouraged to use what Trump himself has hailed as “the ultimate product” can make up their own mind.
